summary: Question: how did David Harding build AHL and Winton and what does he believe about markets? Method: oral-history interview (18 June 2013) covering career, trend-following origins, research method, CTA industry, 2008, equities expansion. Conclusion: markets trend and efficient-market theory is wrong; a diversified rule-based trend system plus empirical research earned returns, but no system works forever and crowding/capacity erodes it, so he diversifies into more markets.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: the market was down 80 percent in the U.K. It was the most dramatic bear market in
claims.claim: Harding recalls the 1974 UK equity bear market as about an 80 percent fall, the worst in UK history, worse than the 1930s.
claims.reported_result: UK equities down about 80% to the 1974 low (recollection, no source); UK market cap $10 billion at the low
claims.testable: partly - verifiable from UK index history

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: of technical analysis, which is not rigorous knowledge at all.
claims.claim: He regarded the technical-analysis literature as a taxonomy of market movements, not rigorous science; he supplemented it with bond/futures mathematics.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: The appeal to me of a commodity broker is they traded in lots of different markets, so I could study the charts not of one market, but of lots of different markets.
claims.claim: Moving from a single market (gilts) to many markets gave more chances for patterns and was the start of his multi-market approach.
claims.testable: partly - breadth effect testable by diversification benefit

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: so there was definitely a move from focusing on one market to focusing on a larger group of markets.
claims.claim: Harding reasons that something may be happening in another market when one is quiet, so a larger market set offers more opportunity.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: We drew 200 charts every day, so we drew at least maybe 200 to 400 charts by hand
claims.claim: At Sabre the team hand-drew 200-400 charts daily and catalogued chart patterns in a craft-like empirical study of markets.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: You had to tick short-term trend, medium-term trend, long-term trend, pattern, seasonal, fundamentals, cumulative volume.
claims.claim: Edwards' 13-point pre-trade checklist included short, medium and long-term trend, pattern, seasonal, fundamentals, cumulative volume and technical indicators; Harding found it sensible as a discipline for deciding to trade.
claims.exact_rule: checklist inputs: short-term trend, medium-term trend, long-term trend, chart pattern, seasonal, fundamentals, cumulative volume, technical indicators (13 points in total, only 7 named)
claims.data_needed: price charts, volume, seasonal and fundamental data
claims.indicator: trend, pattern, seasonal, fundamental, volume checklist

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: really getting a very strong feeling that they trended.
claims.claim: Plotting markets by hand every day gave Harding a strong impression that prices trend, contrary to efficient-market theory.
claims.direction: trend continues: up days followed by up
claims.conditions: subjective impression from daily hand-plotted charts

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: we would take Robin Edwards'
claims.claim: Plan: take Edwards' discretionary method, test it with the physicists' computer systems and turn it into an automated trading system.
claims.exact_rule: codify discretionary chart-pattern method into rules and backtest on computers

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: buy when the market goes through its highest high frame days, and sell when it goes through the lowest low frame days.
claims.claim: Brockham's inherited trading system was a breakout rule: buy on a new highest high over a window of days, sell on a new lowest low (window length not given).
claims.exact_rule: long when price exceeds highest high of last N days; short/exit when price breaks lowest low of last N days; N unstated
claims.data_needed: daily highs and lows per market
claims.direction: buy breakout highs, sell breakdown lows
claims.testable: yes - N unspecified, needs a grid

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: The idea was to computerize, to test and automate Robin Edwards' ideas so as to move
claims.claim: AHL's original goal was to computerize, test and automate Edwards' chart-based ideas.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: it showed you that a very complex process could be partially replicated by a very simple algorithm.
claims.claim: Buy/sell points of the simple breakout rule were close to Edwards' complex pattern method, so a simple algorithm can partly replicate discretionary chart trading.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: In the first half of 1987, there was a very big bull market in silver and so we were up to 50 percent in six months or something.
claims.claim: AHL gained up to about 50 percent in the first half of 1987, helped by a big silver bull market (trend-following profit in one market).
claims.reported_result: up to ~50% in six months, H1 1987 (recollection, 'or something')

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: Management fees were 6 percent a year, and the money started coming in rapidly.
claims.claim: Early AHL management fees were 6 percent a year.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: Mike and Marty wrote the programs for testing trading systems and did the testing of the
claims.claim: Workflow at AHL: programmers built and ran system tests while Harding specified ideas to test.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: I wanted to use computers to research and test trading systems thinking, in my view correctly, that if you are good at that in the end some money's going to find itself your way.
claims.claim: Harding's premise: being good at computer-based research and testing of systems eventually attracts capital.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: that efficient market theory was wrong, that Brownian motion was not a good estimate.
claims.claim: AHL's research showed to Harding that efficient-market theory and Brownian motion were poor descriptions of price behaviour.
claims.conditions: evidence not shown in the talk or the interview
claims.testable: yes - testable: trend/autocorrelation vs random walk

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: What I couldn’t do was present the results that we had on which our trading system was based
claims.claim: He withheld the empirical results behind AHL's system, so the claim that markets are inefficient is unsupported by data in the talk or interview.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: I could at that day have given a definitive disproof of the efficient market theory
claims.claim: Harding asserts his data could have definitively disproved efficient-market theory.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: so you're not studying the underlying reality.
claims.claim: Harding criticizes banks' use of financial mathematics to price derivatives from a model and sell at a markup, since it does not test whether the model matches market reality.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: would study the data and model how markets actually work by studying data
claims.claim: Harding contrasts empiricists, who model markets from data like natural scientists, with theory-driven quants, calling the empiricists a small, derided minority at the time.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: Because I had a very deep understanding of the ideas involved in running trend following trading systems.
claims.claim: Winton (set up 1997) started as a trend-following CTA because Harding already knew how to run those systems.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: we were able to run a CTA just on a spreadsheet program in Excel with three people.
claims.claim: Winton's early trend-following system ran on one Excel spreadsheet with three staff, showing the rules were simple enough to need no programmers.
claims.exact_rule: trend-following CTA run on a single spreadsheet

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: They didn’t work smoothly, but they continued to make money, so some level of success—providing you were not over-leveraged and you stuck to it—some level of success was eventually guaranteed
claims.claim: Trend-following systems developed in the 1980s kept making money, though unevenly, if not over-leveraged and followed consistently.
claims.reported_result: qualitative: kept making money from the 1980s to 2013 (including the dot-com period); no numbers
claims.conditions: requires modest leverage and discipline to stay with the system

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: its virtue is in trends forming in very high capacity.
claims.claim: The key virtue of trend following is very high capacity, since trends exist across whole asset classes, even though returns are not smooth.
claims.testable: partly - capacity measurable by AUM and market-impact data

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: because it's talking about the very exploitable effect in the price movements of whole asset classes.
claims.claim: He sees trend following as a broad effect in whole asset classes, not a small anomaly.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: It's testable because you can bet against the two sides.
claims.claim: Trend-following theory (B) versus the mainstream efficient-market theory (A) differ testably through performance of trading each way.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: very little difference between macro hedge funds and CTAs.
claims.claim: Macro hedge funds and CTAs differ mainly by origin (securities versus commodities business), not by strategy.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: the securities industry needed something to sell that didn’t require stocks to go up so it sold hedge funds.
claims.claim: Early-2000s equity bear market pushed the securities industry to sell hedge funds, which created spillover inflows to CTAs.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: It's about whether you believe in efficient market theory. If you believe in efficient market theory, you don’t invest in CTAs.
claims.claim: Allocators' decision to hold CTAs depends on belief in market efficiency; endowments such as Yale did not invest, about half of hedge fund investors did.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: CTAs had made money in 2001, 2002, so they always looked good when you combined them in optimizers
claims.claim: CTAs made money in the 2001-2002 equity bear market, so mean-variance optimizers added them to portfolios.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: I actually went in when it was relatively unsuccessful.
claims.claim: Winton was relatively unsuccessful in the early 2000s compared to peers like Aspect, which grew on stronger institutional sales.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: because of course in the 2000s bloody commodities started making out like they had in the
claims.claim: Performance in the 2000s was helped by commodities coming back to life as in the 1970s after two dull decades.
claims.reported_result: qualitative; commodities trended in 2000s after ~20 quiet years

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: the track record showed compound growth of 19 percent. It was uncorrelated to other hedge funds in the stock market
claims.claim: Winton's seven-to-eight-year record before 2006 showed 19% compound growth and no correlation with other hedge funds and equities.
claims.reported_result: 19% compound growth over about 7-8 years (to c.2005-06), uncorrelated to hedge funds and stocks; gross/net not stated

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: We had forty-eight months in a row of raising more than fifty million in new assets.
claims.claim: Winton raised over $50 million of new assets in each of 48 consecutive months (to about August 2008), driven by hedge-fund boom and performance.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: The quant quake was caused, supposedly, partly by knock-on effects of credit spreads beginning to balloon.
claims.claim: Harding says the August 2007 quant quake was a canary for the credit crunch, supposedly linked to widening credit spreads.
claims.conditions: August 2007, same week Bear Stearns suspended CDO funds (7 August 2007)

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: we had accumulated large short positions in the stock market because the market had spent the year gradually turning over.
claims.claim: By early 2008 the trend system had built large equity shorts as the market gradually rolled over, and was massively short by the autumn crash.
claims.reported_result: large short equity positions in early 2008, massively short in autumn 2008; made a lot of money in 2007 and 2008

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: Yes, just following trends really. The trends changed slowly. The trends in the market,
claims.claim: Harding explains the 2008 gains as plain trend following: trends changed slowly so the system could follow them.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: the slide in 2008, didn’t come out of the blue. It was a true bear market, a classic bear market, the kind of bear market that creates the need for the term bear market.
claims.claim: The 2008 decline was a gradual classic bear market, which trend followers could capture.
claims.conditions: gradual bear markets vs sudden crashes

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: is that it meant that the 50 percent of people who didn’t invest in CTAs decided they’d been wrong.
claims.claim: The 2008 crash converted CTA sceptics, causing later institutional inflows.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: So we were up a lot in 2008, then we were down in 2009
claims.claim: The system was up a lot in 2008 and down in 2009; assets fell from $16bn to $11bn on hedge-fund redemptions, then grew to about $30bn.
claims.reported_result: 2008 large gain, 2009 loss (no figures); AUM 16bn -> 11bn -> ~30bn; lost a third of AUM in a couple of months after Aug/Sep 2008

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: we were always one and twenty.
claims.claim: Winton core pricing: 1% management fee and 20% performance fee, with distributors adding their own layer.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: We had started off at one and twenty in 1998 and we still broadly have a core pricing of one and twenty now.
claims.claim: Core fees unchanged since 1997-98; a 1-and-20 fee is below industry, though investors via distributors pay more.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: we diversify into 100 exchange traded futures.
claims.claim: The CTA already trades about 100 exchange-traded futures, and more diversification is limited because no more futures markets exist.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: We could do better if we could find more undiversified markets to diversify into.
claims.claim: Adding uncorrelated markets improves results, so Winton moves into equities.
claims.testable: yes - diversification benefit vs number of markets

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: It's not just a question of copying into another thousand markets.
claims.claim: Equity systems are not trend-following copies of the futures rules; the common element is mathematical modelling of prices.
claims.exact_rule: separate models for equities; ~1,000 exchange-traded equity markets as the added universe

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: It's not surprising that you would use mathematics in gambling, because statistics is about calculating the odds.
claims.claim: Investing is handicapping: work out the odds and bet accordingly (Buffett's term).

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: We have a preference for people who have more advanced academic skills and then have them learning about finance than people who have advanced financial skills learning the necessary academic ones.
claims.claim: Winton hires people strong in statistics/modelling and teaches them markets, rather than the reverse.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: to forecast as well as we possibly can the returns, risks, covariance matrices, and transaction costs of the 1100 markets in our portfolio
claims.claim: Winton's research objective: forecast returns, risks, covariances and transaction costs for about 1,100 markets, then build an optimal portfolio.
claims.exact_rule: forecast expected return, volatility, covariance, transaction costs per market; optimize portfolio

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: is easy and forecasting return is hard, and forecasting transaction costs is easy.
claims.claim: Covariance and transaction costs are predictable while returns are hard to forecast.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: the volatility of the stock market is fairly predictable.
claims.claim: Equity volatility (about 12 percent annualized) is fairly predictable, supporting volatility-based risk scaling.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: It could be anything between minus fourteen and plus fourteen, any number in that range, whereas volatility broadly speaking could be between eleven and thirteen or ten and fourteen or something
claims.claim: Illustration: the S&P 500's 20-day return range (about -14% to +14%) is wide while volatility ranges only about 10-14%, so returns are very uncertain and volatility predictable.
claims.reported_result: 20-day S&P return could be -14% to +14%; volatility 10-14% (illustrative, not a statistic)

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: look for explanatory variables, which means things that might explain what the market's going to do in the future and we research the conditional probability distribution
claims.claim: Research method: search for explanatory variables and estimate the conditional probability distribution of returns given them.
claims.exact_rule: estimate conditional distribution of future returns given explanatory variables

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: Is the trend likely to continue or reverse, is it likely to go up or down in spring or summer, or before Christmas or after bank holidays?
claims.claim: Example variables: trend continuation versus reversal, seasonality (season, pre-Christmas, bank holidays), soy-corn gap, hog-corn ratio, oil/natural gas spread, bond-equity relation, mean reversion.
claims.exact_rule: candidate explanatory variables listed, no thresholds given
claims.indicator: trend, seasonality, soy/corn gap, hog/corn ratio, oil vs gas spread, bond-equity relation, mean reversion

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: investigate which is through proper analysis of data, not just buying and putting your finger in the air
claims.claim: Markets should be studied through proper data analysis rather than gut feel.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: There are no immutable eternal truths at all.
claims.claim: Financial markets are social science with no fixed laws, so patterns can change once investigated or traded.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: In fact, the efficient market theory is the idea of a physical law.
claims.claim: Efficient-market theory wrongly treats markets as governed by physical law, a trap for scientists entering finance.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: you can trace the critical intellectual property in those firms back to the founding of AHL.
claims.claim: Most large CTAs trace their intellectual property to AHL, apart from Transtrend and Lynx, so systems across the industry are similar.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: When too much money is put into something usually it works less well.
claims.claim: Trend following is subject to capacity decay; no strategy works forever.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: as fast as the industry is growing you'd expect it to work less well, and one of the ways to compensate for that is to diversify further.
claims.claim: With the CTA industry growing, trend following should degrade; diversification to more markets compensates.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: If we could make let's say twenty basis points more than that then that is worth literally billions
claims.claim: Harding thinks mathematical methods could beat a cap-weighted index like the S&P 500 by about 20 basis points, which would be worth billions in fees.
claims.reported_result: target +20 bp over S&P 500 long-only (aspiration, not a result)

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: this efficient market theory which is used to justify that is an idea which is wrong because it's based upon the idea that this field is physics.
claims.claim: Harding says the efficient-market justification for indexing is wrong because it assumes market laws like physics, though he accepts that low-cost broad indexes beat most active managers.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: you incrementally improve something that is already well in use in the world's infrastructure.
claims.claim: Business approach: improve an existing widely used product such as the index incrementally rather than replace it.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: they like to sell a finished system. This is a complete fallacy.
claims.claim: A static finished trading system cannot work for decades; investors need a research team continuously updating methods.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: we've got a $300 million long-only business
claims.claim: Winton's long-only equity business was about $300 million after three years of a ten-year build.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: no fixed system that will work from now to the end of eternity.
claims.claim: Systems must change through time; Harding expects the 2013 methods to differ from those 17 years later.

claims.speaker: David Harding (DH)
claims.quote: they're investing in a system that has been widely gamed.
claims.claim: Harding says the S&P 500 index approach has been exploited by traders who buy before index additions and sell before deletions, hurting index investors.
claims.conditions: ~15 years to 2013 of weak S&P 500 returns per his statement
